summary:
Judges covers the generations between Joshua's death and Israel's first kings. After the conquest generation dies, "another generation rose up who did not know the LORD or the works that He had done for Israel" (2:10), and the book lays out its own recurring pattern (2:11–19): Israel serves the Baals (local forms of the Canaanite storm god), the LORD hands them over to plunderers, they cry out, and He raises up a judge — Hebrew shophet, here a military deliverer and leader, not a courtroom figure. When a judge died, the people "became even more corrupt than their fathers" (2:19). Twelve judges are named.

Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, assassinates Eglon king of Moab with a hidden double-edged sword (3:15–30). Deborah, a prophetess and the only judge shown holding court — Israel "would go up to her for judgment" at the Palm of Deborah (4:5) — sends Barak against Sisera's nine hundred chariots of iron; Sisera flees and dies in the tent of Jael, a tent peg through his temple. Gideon tears down his father's altar to Baal by night and routs Midian with three hundred men, then makes an ephod (a priestly vestment) from the golden spoils; Israel worships it, "and it became a snare to Gideon and his household" (8:27). Jephthah vows that if God grants victory over the Ammonites he will offer up "whatever comes out the door of my house"; his daughter, his only child, comes out dancing, and "he did to her as he had vowed" (11:31, 39). Whether she was sacrificed, as the plain wording suggests, or dedicated to lifelong virginity is debated.

Samson is a Nazirite from birth, set apart to God by vow: no wine, no contact with a corpse, no razor to the head (Numbers 6:1–8). He fights the Philistines single-handedly while breaking his vow piece by piece. After Delilah coaxes out the secret of his hair, he is blinded and set to grinding grain in a Gaza prison; when his hair regrows, he collapses the temple packed for a sacrifice to the Philistine god Dagon: "in his death he killed more than he had killed in his life" (16:30). Yet Hebrews 11:32 lists Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah as examples of faith.

The last five chapters drop the cycle for two accounts of collapse from within. Micah of Ephraim builds a household shrine around a silver idol and hires a Levite (a member of Israel's priestly tribe) as priest; the migrating tribe of Dan then takes both idol and priest for itself (17–18). Next a Levite's concubine (a secondary wife) is raped through the night and left dead at Gibeah, in an episode that mirrors Sodom (Genesis 19:4–8); the war that follows nearly annihilates the tribe of Benjamin (19–21). Four times these chapters note that Israel had no king, a line often read as looking ahead to the monarchy of 1–2 Samuel, though others take the missing king to be God Himself. The full refrain closes the book: "In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (17:6; 21:25).
